sections.title: Booking a holiday cottage in Cornwall
sections.context: You will hear a man phoning a holiday letting agency to book a cottage in Cornwall.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: Good morning, Seaview Cottages, Bethan speaking. How can I help?

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: Good morning. I'm hoping to book a cottage for the summer holidays. I saw one on your website, but I'm not sure whether it's still available.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: Of course. Let me take a few details first, and then we can look at it together. Could I have your name, please?

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: Yes, it's Quentin Thackeray.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: Could you spell your surname for me?

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: Certainly. T-H-A-C-K-E-R-A-Y. Thackeray, like the novelist.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: T-H-A-C-K-E-R-A-Y. Thank you, Mr Thackeray. Which cottage were you interested in?

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: I think it was called Honeysuckle Cottage, the one with the blue door and the garden going down to the water.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: Ah, I'm sorry, Honeysuckle is already taken for the whole of July. But I have a very similar cottage in the same village. It's called Primrose Cottage, and it also has a garden that leads to the harbour wall.

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: That sounds just as good. Is there a bedroom for each of the children? We have three.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: There are three bedrooms, one double and two twins, so that works well. When would you like to arrive?

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: I was thinking of Saturday 5 July.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: Hmm, let me check. I'm afraid Primrose isn't free that weekend. A family is staying until the eleventh. The first Saturday available is 12 July.

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: That's fine, actually. The schools break up a week later than I thought, so 12 July is better.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: Lovely. And how long would you like to stay? Most people take a full week, from Saturday to Saturday.

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: We'd like a bit longer, if possible. Perhaps fourteen nights.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: Hold on, let me look at the calendar. Ah, someone else has booked it from the twenty-sixth, so you could stay up to the twenty-second at most. That would be 10 nights, from the twelfth to the twenty-second.

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: Then 10 nights it is. That's fine.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: Perfect. How many people will be staying?

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: Five of us. Myself, my wife and the three children. Oh, and my mother has just said she would like to join us, so it will be 6.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: Six is no problem. The cottage sleeps up to eight.

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: And what's the price?

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: For a week in July it's normally £680. But I should explain how it works. The cheaper rate applies only until the end of June. From the first of July the cottages move into the high season, so the weekly price goes up to £720. For ten nights, we calculate it by the day, so I'll work out the total for you in a moment.

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: All right. So £720 is the figure for July.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: That's right, per week. I'll send you the full total by email. Now, are you bringing any pets?

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: We'd like to bring our dog. She's a small spaniel, and very well behaved.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: That's fine. We allow one dog in this cottage, and there's an extra charge of £25 for the stay. It covers cleaning.

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: That seems reasonable.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: Did you want to know about the beaches?

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: Yes, please. The children are keen on swimming.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: The nearest beach is Polgwidden Cove. That's spelled P-O-L-G-W-I-D-D-E-N. It's about ten minutes on foot, down the lane behind the cottage. It's sandy, and there are rock pools at low tide. There are bigger beaches a few miles away, but they get very crowded in the summer.

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: Polgwidden Cove sounds perfect.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: One thing to mention is that dogs aren't allowed on the cove between May and September. But there's a path along the cliffs where she can run.

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: Oh, that's a shame, but we'll manage. How do we collect the key?

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: There's no need to come to the office. The key is in a safe beside the back door. The code is 4719. I'll confirm it in writing nearer the date.

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: 4719. Good. And when can we arrive?

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: The cottage is normally ready from 3:00, but the cleaners are very busy on a Saturday, so I would plan for 4:30 to be safe. If you arrive earlier, you can leave your bags in the garden shed.

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: 4:30 is fine. Thank you very much.

transcript.speaker: Bethan
transcript.text: I'll send the booking form by email, and a deposit is due within seven days. Thank you for calling, Mr Thackeray.

transcript.speaker: Quentin
transcript.text: Thank you. Goodbye.

sections.title: Leith Harbour Food Festival
sections.context: You will hear an organiser welcoming volunteers and visitors to a food festival in Edinburgh.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the briefing for the Leith Harbour Food Festival. I'm Morag, the festival manager, and I want to run through the main points so that you can answer visitors' questions. The festival takes place over three days, from Friday to Sunday, and we expect about twelve thousand visitors.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: First, the opening hours. The programme says we open at ten o'clock on Friday, but that has changed. Several of the stallholders are travelling from the Highlands, and the delivery trucks can't reach the site until the morning, so we won't open until noon. On Saturday and Sunday we open at ten as usual. Please tell visitors that if they ask.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: Now, how do visitors pay? Entry to the festival is free. Inside, you can buy full meals from the stalls, and most of them accept cards. But the small tastings, the samples that cost a pound or two, work differently. Visitors buy tokens at the main gate. A strip of ten tokens costs eight pounds, and each tasting takes one or two tokens. That keeps the queues moving, and it also means the stalls don't have to handle a lot of coins.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: Another change concerns the cookery theatre. Last year it was in the big white tent near the water, but that was damaged in the winter storms and the cost of repair was too high. So we've moved the theatre to the old warehouse behind the market. Please make sure that you give visitors directions, because the signs at the gate haven't been updated yet. Some visitors may think it's moved because of noise from the stage, but that's not the reason.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: Waste is a big issue for us. All the hot drinks are served in cups that can be composted, but we'd prefer to use none at all. So if visitors bring their own reusable cup, we give them fifty pence off the price of a drink. It's not much, but people seem to like it, and we gave away hundreds last year.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: Finally, our main theme. Many festivals raise money for charity, and a few focus on training young chefs. Those are good aims, but this year our priority is education. On Friday morning, before we open to the public, six primary schools will visit, and each class will meet a farmer, handle fresh ingredients and make a simple lunch. The purpose is to show children where their food comes from. So if you see groups of children on Friday, please be extra patient.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: Now let me take you round the site, so you know what's where. We're standing at the main gate. If you walk straight ahead, you'll reach the Harbour Market. For years this was famous for fish, and you might expect to find a seafood tasting there. That was cancelled this year because the main supplier withdrew. Instead, the market will be full of farmers selling their vegetables directly to the public, with no shop in between. Prices are lower, and the produce is usually picked the same morning.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: Turn left at the market and you'll find the Orchard Tent. This is a new addition. About a dozen fruit growers from Fife and the Borders have come, and visitors can taste apple, pear and plum juices, and talk to the people who grew them. The most popular drink last year was a cloudy apple juice with a hint of ginger. I'd recommend it to anyone who asks.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: Next to the Orchard Tent is the Cookery Theatre, as I explained, in the old warehouse. It has seats for two hundred people, and chefs from restaurants across Scotland will cook in front of the audience. Visitors can watch and ask questions, but they don't take part. If a visitor wants to join in a baking session, I'm afraid we haven't organised one this year. We hope to have it next time.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: On the far side of the market you'll see Street Food Row, a long line of vans and small kitchens. They serve dishes from all over the world: Indian curry, Mexican tacos, Polish dumplings and many more. It gets very busy at lunchtime, so I'd advise visitors to go early, or to try it on Sunday when it's quieter.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: And right at the end, beside the old lighthouse, is the Dairy Corner. Here you can taste cheeses made on small farms across Scotland, from soft cream cheeses to a very strong blue one that is quite an acquired taste. Each stall will give you a small piece, and if you like it, you can buy a whole one to take home.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: A few practical points. First aid is in the blue cabin by the gate. Lost children should be brought there, too. Toilets are on both sides of the market. All volunteers wear a green T-shirt, and you should have your badge on at all times. If anything goes wrong, my phone number is on the back of the badge.

transcript.speaker: Morag
transcript.text: Lunch for volunteers is served at one o'clock in the staff tent, and there's free tea and coffee all day. I'd ask you to be friendly, patient and above all enthusiastic. Visitors remember a smile far longer than they remember the exact answer. Right, are there any questions before we begin?

sections.title: A marketing project for a local brewery
sections.context: You will hear two business students discussing a marketing project with their tutor.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: Hello, Callie. Hello, Rohan. Come in. I've been looking forward to hearing how the brewery project is going. Remind me, which company did you choose in the end?

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: Harrow Lane Brewery. We chose it because it has just launched an alcohol-free beer, and we wanted to see how a small company introduces a completely new product.

transcript.speaker: Rohan
transcript.text: Originally I was in favour of a bigger firm, because we'd have more data. But a new launch gives us a clear question, so I think Callie was right.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: A sensible choice. New products are the best place to study marketing. And what have you done so far?

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: We designed a questionnaire and sent it to about two hundred people in the city. We got ninety-four replies.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: That's a respectable response rate. Were there any problems with the questions?

transcript.speaker: Rohan
transcript.text: Yes. Some of the people who replied weren't in the target group at all. The brewery wants to reach adults between twenty-five and forty, but about a third of our replies came from students who were under twenty-one. We should have checked that at the start.

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: I'd say that was a bigger problem than the wording. A few questions were confusing, but we fixed those after the first twenty replies.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: You can simply exclude the younger replies, as long as you explain why. Now, let me ask about the results. Did anything surprise you?

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: Two things, really. The first was that most people had never heard of the brewery. We assumed that, being local, it would be well known, but over sixty per cent said they didn't recognise the name.

transcript.speaker: Rohan
transcript.text: And the other surprise was about price. We expected that cost would be the main factor, but it was only the third most important reason for choosing a drink. Taste and the look of the bottle came first.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: Interesting. What about the differences between men and women? Many studies suggest women are less likely to try alcohol-free beer.

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: We found the opposite, but the difference was too small to mean anything. And the age groups were about the same.

transcript.speaker: Rohan
transcript.text: There was one more thing, but it wasn't a surprise. Most people preferred bottles to cans.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: That's well known, so I wouldn't spend time on it. Did you also speak to anyone at the brewery?

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: Yes, we interviewed the owner, Mrs Dalgleish, for half an hour. She was very open about the sales figures, but she asked us not to publish them.

transcript.speaker: Rohan
transcript.text: So we'll show them only as percentages, and I think that's acceptable.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: It is, provided you tell your reader that you've done it. Keep a copy of her written permission as well.

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: She emailed us last week, so we have that.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: Good. Now, the recommendations. The company has a small budget. What do you suggest?

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: We thought about five options. The first was advertising on social media. At first I was keen, but when I looked at the cost, it was far more than they can afford. Even a small campaign costs thousands.

transcript.speaker: Rohan
transcript.text: Local radio is cheaper, but the listeners are mostly older. So it's not a good match with the target group.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: And tasting events?

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: That was the most popular idea in our survey. Respondents said they'd be more willing to try the beer if they could taste it first. The only difficulty is that someone from the brewery has to stand there all afternoon, and they only have three employees.

transcript.speaker: Rohan
transcript.text: Discount vouchers have already been tried by almost every other drinks company in the area, so customers are used to them. They don't create much excitement any more.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: And the last one?

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: Changing the label on the bottle. Here we have to be careful, because there are rules about what you can claim on alcohol-free products. For example, they can't say the drink is healthy. The brewery would have to check with a lawyer.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: That's a good point, and many students miss it. I suppose you also considered the tourist season?

transcript.speaker: Rohan
transcript.text: Yes, the summer is the busiest time, and the tasting events would work very well then, since visitors are looking for local products.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: Excellent. Now, about the report. I'd like your recommendations to come near the beginning, not at the end. Many readers only read the first page. And please keep the literature review short. Two pages is plenty.

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: Should we include the raw questionnaire in the appendix?

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: Yes, but not the individual answers, only the questions. And remember to mention the limits of your sample. Ninety-four replies isn't large, and you removed some of them.

transcript.speaker: Rohan
transcript.text: We'll make sure we do that. Should we also compare the brewery with a competitor?

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: Only if you have time. One company studied properly is better than two done badly.

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: Is it all right if we include a short section on what we would do with a larger budget?

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: Briefly, yes. But keep it to one paragraph. The marker wants to see that you can work within the limits you were given.

transcript.speaker: Rohan
transcript.text: That makes sense. We'll keep it short.

transcript.speaker: Professor Ellis
transcript.text: Good. Send me a draft by the end of next week, and I'll give you feedback within three days. Well done so far.

transcript.speaker: Callie
transcript.text: Thank you, Professor.

transcript.speaker: Rohan
transcript.text: Thanks very much.

sections.title: Tidal power
sections.context: You will hear an engineering lecturer talking about how the energy of the tides can be used to produce electricity.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about an energy source that is more predictable than almost any other: the tides. Britain is surrounded by water, and it has some of the biggest tides in the world, so it's no surprise that engineers have been dreaming of harnessing them for more than a century. Let me start with the basic science.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, although the Sun plays a smaller part. As the Earth turns, the Moon's pull drags the oceans into a bulge on the side nearest to it. There's a second bulge on the opposite side. The result is that in most places there are two high tides and two low tides. Because the Moon is moving round the Earth at the same time, a full cycle takes about 25 hours, not twenty-four. That is why tide times move later each day.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The difference in height between high and low tide is called the tidal range. In the open ocean it's small, but in certain shaped coastlines the water is funnelled and the range becomes enormous. The Bristol Channel and the Severn Estuary have one of the largest tidal ranges anywhere in the world, up to fourteen metres. That makes them very attractive for energy.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The first type of technology is the tidal barrage. A barrage is a long wall built across an estuary, rather like a dam. At high tide, water flows in through gates, and when the tide goes out the water is released through turbines, which generate electricity. The best known example is La Rance, in northern France. It opened in 1966 and has operated for more than half a century. In fact, for many years it was the largest tidal power station on Earth.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So why don't we have barrages everywhere? The main answer is the environment. A barrage changes the flow of water in the whole estuary. The mudflats, which are the feeding grounds for thousands of wading birds, may be covered for longer, or may no longer be exposed at all. Fish migration is another concern, because salmon and eels must pass through the turbines. For the Severn, a barrage has been proposed several times, but each time it has been rejected, because the cost was enormous and the damage to wildlife was considered too great.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That leads me to the second technology, which is much more popular today: tidal stream turbines. These look very similar to wind turbines. They have large blades fixed to a tower, but the tower stands on the sea floor and the blades are turned by moving water, rather than by air. Water is about 800 times denser than air, so even a slow current has a lot of power. A turbine with blades only half the size of a wind turbine can produce the same amount of electricity.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The best sites are places where the tide runs fast through a narrow channel. A good example is the Pentland Firth, between the north of Scotland and the Orkney Islands. There, the current can reach 5 metres per second, but most turbines need only around 3 metres per second to work efficiently. The first array of turbines was installed there in 2016, and it now supplies electricity to thousands of homes.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: What are the advantages? The first is certainty. Unlike wind or sunshine, the tides can be predicted, and engineers can forecast the output of a tidal plant for decades in advance. We know when the next high tide will be in the year 2100. Compare that to the weather, which can change within hours. The second advantage is that the machines are mostly hidden below the surface, so they don't spoil the view, and there is less opposition from local residents.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And the disadvantages? The most important is cost. Building and installing a turbine in strong currents is difficult and expensive, and the equipment has to survive corrosion, storms and marine growth. Even more important in the long term is maintenance. A turbine on the sea floor can only be reached by ship, and in rough weather that may be impossible for weeks. So the total cost of the electricity is still higher than from a wind farm.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: There's also the question of marine life. Early studies suggested that seals and fish could be injured by moving blades. More recent monitoring has found that most animals avoid the turbines, but we need more evidence, especially in the case of larger arrays.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Where does the technology go from here? Some engineers are developing floating turbines, which are attached to the surface by cables and are much cheaper to install. Others are looking at tidal lagoons, which are walls enclosing a smaller area of water, away from the main estuary, so the effect on wildlife is smaller. Whether they will work at scale is still an open question.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: To sum up, tidal power is not going to solve our energy problems alone. But because of its reliability, it may be a very useful partner to wind and solar. In next week's lecture, we will look at wave power, and ask whether the same arguments apply. Thank you.
